Safeguards — sessions, web surface and appearance

The protections on the browser-facing side of SATOM — security headers, CSRF, rate limits, account lockout, anti-lockout and two-factor sign-in — and why operator theming accepts design tokens, never raw CSS.

👤 ForAdministratorAdvanced user
📍 WhereSign-in and every authenticated page; Settings → Appearance
On this page
  • Sessions and the web surface
  • Operator-supplied appearance

Sessions and the web surface#

Guard What it prevents
Content-Security-Policy with a per-request nonce Injected script running. Inline event attributes are blocked outright, so an injected on… handler is inert.
Framing, sniffing and referrer headers Click-jacking and content-type confusion. Framing is denied, MIME sniffing is off and the referrer is restricted (strict-origin-when-cross-origin).
Authenticated pages are never cached A stale page or menu surviving a deployment in the browser.
CSRF protection Cross-site request forgery — application-wide, including the JSON endpoints the UI drives.
Per-IP rate limits Password guessing from one address. Sign-in (5 per minute), the second-factor challenge (10 per minute), password recovery (5 and 10 per 15 minutes) and the public API each have their own budget.
Per-account lockout A distributed attack on one account, which an IP limit alone cannot isolate. Ten failed sign-ins lock the account for 15 minutes.
Local accounts never fall through to the directory A directory account with the same name taking over the built-in administrator.
Anti-lockout on access administration Losing every administrator. A change that would leave zero active administrators is refused.
Two-factor authentication Sign-in with a stolen password. Local accounts use TOTP with backup codes; directory accounts do MFA at the directory.

See Security model for the full picture, and Authentication and Users and profiles for the settings involved.

Operator-supplied appearance#

Letting an operator recolour the console means accepting operator input into a stylesheet that carries the page's own security nonce. The design of the theme engine follows from refusing to do that naively. See Appearance for how to use it.

Guard What it prevents
Tokens, never raw CSS Stored CSS injection: one closing brace ends the intended rule and starts an attacker's. The editable surface is a closed list of design tokens the stylesheet already exposes — not a text area.
Validated by kind, plus a forbidden-character list A value that is syntactically a colour but semantically a payload. The two layers are not redundant: the colour pattern is narrow enough to stand alone, but shadow and font values accept letters, digits and parentheses — enough to smuggle an external reference past a per-type check.
Gradients parsed structurally The same, for a value type that legitimately contains commas, percentages and nested functions. A gradient must be a linear or radial gradient with an optional direction and two to eight colour stops.
Re-validated when emitted Trusting the database as a boundary. A restore, a replica or a direct SQL session can put a value in the table that never passed the form.
Contrast audited with alpha composition An unreadable console. Every text/background pair is scored; below the legibility floor (3.0:1) the save requires an explicit acknowledgement. The shipped palettes are checked in the test suite, so a change that degrades them fails.
Three independent ways back Lock-out. Revert to the shipped look, activate a built-in theme, or run satom execute reset theme from a shell. Built-in themes cannot be edited or deleted, and deleting the active theme falls back instead of leaving the console unthemed.
The token registry is generated from the stylesheet An editor that silently loses a control. A hand-maintained list would be a copy; the build fails if the two drift.
Every built-in theme declares its own brand ramps An amber console painting blue buttons. A theme stores only its overrides, so a theme that omitted a gradient would inherit the stylesheet's — correct for the default palette, wrong for every other. Built-in themes are also reconciled on start-up, while operator themes stay insert-only.
Gradients are refused where a browser would drop them A border that disappears instead of changing colour. Paint properties accept a gradient; border-color and similar properties silently discard it.
Brand assets: bare file name only, SVG sanitised, raster images re-encoded A stored path escaping the branding folder, and script-carrying SVG reaching the page.

⚠️Warning — There is no dark console

This is stated rather than implied. Status badges and many decorative tints are still literal colour values in the stylesheet, so a dark canvas would leave islands of light. The public website does offer a dark theme — its palette was fully converted to tokens first, which is the work the console still owes.
